title: Bishop and knight III: the whole mate
summary: From any position to mate: the edge, the right corner and Delétang's triangles.
part.netsMate.title: The plan and the nets
part.netsMate.summary: The three stages of the mate and Delétang's nets, down to the mate in the corner.
part.closing.title: Closing the triangles
part.closing.summary: When the bishop jumps to the shorter diagonal, and how the net shrinks into the corner.
part.fromStart.title: From the start to the corner
part.fromStart.summary: The wall that drives the king to the edge and the knight that keeps it out of the wrong corner.
part.fullRules.title: Dangers and the whole mate
part.fullRules.summary: Stalemate, the fifty-move rule and the whole mate against the machine.
step.t_start: The black king is in the middle of the eighth rank and your pieces are still at home. Before moving, make the plan: which corner must the black king go to, and in what stages?
step.t_start.hint1: The mate only exists in the corner of the bishop's colour. First the edge, then the right corner, then the net.
step.intro: You already know the W manoeuvre, and you know how to drive the black king from the middle of the board to the edge. Today we put it all into one plan, from any position: first the edge, then the corner of the bishop's colour, then the mate. And I will show you a second road, which many find easier to remember: Delétang's triangles.
step.net1: Look at the b1–h7 diagonal. The bishop on g6 closes the whole diagonal: the black king cannot cross it. The knight on e6 and my king on f4 plug the dark squares next to it. What is left for the black king is a triangle, from c1 to h1 to h6. That is the first triangle, the big one.
step.net2: The bishop jumped to h5, on the d1–h5 diagonal, and the triangle shrank: now the black king lives between e1, h1 and h4. The knight on e4 plugs f2 and g3; my king on f4 closes the rest. Second triangle, the middle one.
step.net3: The third and last: the bishop on f1 closes the f1–h3 diagonal, the knight on e4 covers f2 and g3, and my king on e2 watches f1 and f2. The black king only has g1, h1 and h2. From here the mate comes by itself.
step.mate: Deliver the mate. The knight reaches for h2 by way of g5, the king closes f2 and the bishop lands the final blow on g2.
step.mate.hint: First the knight to g5: from there it reaches f3 and covers h2. Then the king on f2, the knight on f3 with check, and the bishop on g2.
step.mate.done: Mate. Look at the picture: king on f2, knight on f3, bishop on g2. It is always the same, in any corner of the bishop's colour.
step.t_shrink: The black king is trapped near h1. Which bishop move tightens the net without leaving any way out?
step.t_shrink.hint1: Check which squares the black king can still reach. If it cannot get to the shorter diagonal, the bishop can jump to it.
step.shrink: Each phase asks one question: when may the bishop jump to the smaller diagonal? Answer: when the black king can no longer reach the new diagonal. Here the black king is on g2, the knight on e4 covers f2 and g3, and my king on f4 covers f3. The d1–h5 diagonal is free for the bishop.
step.close2.hint: The bishop needs a square on the d1–h5 diagonal that the black king does not attack.
step.close2.done: That's it. The black king is left with few squares. Now my king comes in and squeezes, and the bishop waits for the moment to jump again.
step.close3: Now the third. The black king is on g1, the knight covers f2 and g3, my king covers f1 and f2. The bishop has to close the f1–h3 diagonal without being captured. Two moves: close, then adjust.
step.close3.hint: Bishop to h3 closes the diagonal. If the black king goes to h2 and attacks the bishop, it slides back to f1, on the same diagonal.
step.close3.done: Perfect. The black king only has g1, h1 and h2. You already know how to finish from here.
step.edge: Now from the beginning. The black king in the centre, and my pieces still asleep. The order is this: the bishop takes the long diagonal, my king goes to the centre, the knight comes last. Together they build a wall, and the black king goes to the edge.
step.wall: Build the wall. Bishop on the long diagonal, king to the centre, knight to the centre, and the bishop closes the wall.
step.wall.hint: Bishop to g2, king to d2 and then e3, knight to d3, bishop to e4. Each move takes squares from the black king.
step.wall.done: See the wall? Bishop on e4, knight on d3, king on e3. The black king cannot come back to the centre. From here it goes to a corner, and you know what to do in each one.
step.corner: With a light-squared bishop, the black king will run to h8, the wrong corner. The knight stops it: on f7 it covers h8 and h6. From there you have two roads: the W manoeuvre, which you already know, or locking the king behind the a2–g8 diagonal and closing the three triangles down to a8.
step.play1: This is the position of Delétang's method. The black king can no longer cross the b1–h7 diagonal. Close the three triangles and mate on h1. The machine defends as well as it can; you have moves to spare.
step.t_rhine: Near the right corner, a knight check looks natural here. Before checking, look at the bishop's safety and the black king's squares. What can go wrong?
step.t_rhine.hint1: Imagine the check and find the square the black king runs to. What does it attack from there?
step.traps: Three dangers. First, stalemate: here the check on b6 looks natural, but after Kd8 the black king attacks the bishop; every bishop move stalemates, and losing the bishop is an instant draw. Second, the fifty-move rule: the whole mate takes up to thirty-three moves, so there is no time to wander. Third, the bishop: without it there is no mate.
step.rules: Keep three rules. One: the black king goes to the edge and then to the corner of the bishop's colour, never the other way round. Two: the bishop closes the diagonal; the knight and the king plug the dark squares beside it. Three: the bishop only jumps to the smaller diagonal when the black king can no longer reach it. With that, the whole mate fits inside the fifty moves with room to spare.
step.play2: Now the whole mate. Black king in the centre, your pieces on the first rank. Edge, right corner, mate. Count the moves: you have fifty and need fewer than thirty-five.
ex.e01: White to play. The black king is in the right corner. Deliver the mate.
ex.e01.hint: The black king only has a8. Which piece attacks a8 with your king's protection?
ex.e01.solution: Bb7 is mate: the bishop attacks a8, the king on c7 protects b7 and covers b8, and the knight on c6 covers a7. This is the picture you repeat in any corner of the bishop's colour.
ex.e02: White to play and win. The black king is locked in the third triangle. Bring the knight to the mating square.
ex.e02.hint: The knight needs to reach c6 with check. Which way?
ex.e02.solution: Nb4 takes the knight to c6. After Ka7, Nc6 gives check and pushes the king back to a8, and Bb7 is mate. The bishop on c8 and the king on c7 hold the black king while the knight goes round.
ex.e03: White to play and win. The knight and the bishop are already in place; the king is missing. Three moves.
ex.e03.hint: The black king still has a7 and b8, and the bishop already covers b7. Bring your king closer to take b8; then the knight checks and the bishop finishes.
ex.e03.solution: Kc7 closes b7 and b8. After Ka7, Nc6 gives check and the king goes back to a8; Bb7 is mate. The same picture as on h1, only turned around.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The knight on d3 and the king on g6 are already in place. Which bishop move closes the first triangle?
ex.e04.hint: The first triangle's diagonal runs from a2 to g8. The bishop must stand on it, on a safe square.
ex.e04.solution: Bb3 puts the bishop on the a2–g8 diagonal, and the black king is locked in the a2–a8–g8 triangle. Any safe square on the diagonal will do: a2, c4, f7 or g8 work the same. The knight on d3 covers b4 and c5; the king on g6 covers f6, f7 and g7.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The knight on d5 already covers b6 and c7. Close the second triangle.
ex.e05.hint: The second triangle's diagonal runs from a4 to e8. Where does the bishop enter it without being attacked?
ex.e05.solution: Ba4 closes the a4–e8 diagonal. The black king on a6 cannot reach b5 or c6, which the king on c5 and the bishop cover, and it is locked between a4, a8 and e8. Then the white king pushes, and the bishop jumps to a6–c8.
ex.e06: White to play and win. The bishop wants to go to a4 and close the second triangle, but not yet. What is the move?
ex.e06.hint: If the bishop goes to a4 now, the black king escapes through d5. Who plugs d5?
ex.e06.solution: Ke6 first: the white king covers d5 and d6, and only then may the bishop go to a4. The rule: the bishop only changes diagonal when the black king can no longer reach the new one. Here a king move was missing.
ex.e07: White to play and win. A knight check seems to push the king into the corner. Don't fall for the trap.
ex.e07.hint: After Nb6 check and Kd8, the black king attacks the bishop, and every bishop move stalemates.
ex.e07.solution: Nb6 check is the trap Frederick Rhine published: Kd8 attacks the bishop; if it leaves, it is stalemate; if it stays, the king takes it and it is a draw. Instead, a quiet move: Bb5 keeps the bishop safe on the a4–e8 diagonal, and the black king stays locked. Ba4, Bc6, Na5 or Ke7 win just the same.
ex.e08: White to play and win. The second triangle is closed. Now the king does the work. Where to?
ex.e08.hint: The black king wants e1. The knight covers f2 and g3, and e2 is already covered; your king must take e1 away without getting in the bishop's way.
ex.e08.solution: Kd2 takes e1 from the black king, which is pushed to g1 or g2. The bishop on g4 keeps closing d1–h5, and the knight on e4 covers f2 and g3. In a few moves the bishop will be able to jump to h3.
ex.e09: White to play and win. Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013: the black king tries to flee along the f-file. Which move keeps the net?
ex.e09.hint: The knight on d4 covers e2 and f3. Which knight jump covers f4 and g3 instead, closing the way out to the middle of the board?
ex.e09.solution: Ne2 is the W manoeuvre move: the knight covers f4 and g3, and the black king cannot escape along the f-file. In the game, Ushenina played Bd5, the black king fled through g3 and g4, and the game ended drawn by the fifty-move rule. Bf7 also keeps the net, by another road.
ex.e10: White to play and win. The black king runs to h8, the wrong corner for the light-squared bishop. Stop it.
ex.e10.hint: Which piece can cover h8 and h6 at the same time?
ex.e10.solution: Nf7 covers h8 and h6: the black king can only go back to f8, away from the wrong corner. From there you choose: the W manoeuvre to a8, or locking the king behind the a2–g8 diagonal and closing the triangles. Ng6 also covers h8 and wins, one move slower.
ex.e11: White to play and win. The first triangle is closed and the black king is pirouetting inside it. Three king moves to squeeze.
ex.e11.hint: The bishop and the knight stay where they are. Your king walks round underneath, through d1, d2 and d3, always glued to the black king.
ex.e11.solution: Kd1, Kd2 and Kd3: the white king enters the triangle and pushes the black king to the right, towards h1. The bishop on g6 holds the b1–h7 diagonal and the knight on e6 covers d4 and f4. With the black king against the h-file, the bishop jumps to h5 and the second triangle is born.
key.net1: Delétang's first triangle, the big one: bishop on g6 on the b1–h7 diagonal, knight on e6 and king on f4. From the Wikipedia example, which follows Pandolfini.
key.net2: The second triangle, the middle one: bishop on h5 on the d1–h5 diagonal, knight on e4 and king on f4.
key.net3: The third triangle, the small one: bishop on f1 on the f1–h3 diagonal, knight on e4 and king on e2. The black king only has g1, h1 and h2.
key.deletangStart: The position Wikipedia uses to show Delétang's method: the black king can no longer cross the b1–h7 diagonal.
key.rhineTrap: The stalemate trap noted by Frederick Rhine in 2000, according to Wikipedia: Nb6 check and Kd8, and White no longer wins.
key.practiceStart: The starting position of the Lichess practice (arex): the whole mate from the first rank.
history: Philidor showed in 1777 how to drive the king out of the wrong corner: that is the W manoeuvre. In October 1922, in Buenos Aires, the Frenchman Daniel Delétang wrote the article "Mat avec le Fou et le Cavalier", published in the magazine La Stratégie in February 1923: three triangles, the big, the middle and the small one, each closed by a bishop diagonal. It is not the shortest road, but it is the one you never forget, and it fits inside the fifty moves. The ending shows up about once in six thousand games, and even grandmasters stumble: Anna Ushenina, then world champion, could not deliver the mate against Olga Girya in Geneva, 2013, and the game was drawn by the fifty-move rule. Tal Shaked, on the other hand, mated Morozevich at the 1997 World Junior Championship and won the title with it.
practice: Enough script. The black king is already near h1, the right corner. Close the triangles or play the W, as you prefer, and deliver the mate. Then the same ending in the speedrun, against the clock.
